name: Aisha Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aisha, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Greenfold Homes, a not-for-profit builder that fixes up old terraced houses so they're warm and cheap to heat. This month we're on Brook Street, pulling up rotten floorboards, putting insulation under, laying new boards, fitting window boards and doors. I'm a trainee, so Ollie, who runs our crew, gives me the cutting list and checks my work, and I still get things wrong. Before this I cooked in a school canteen for twenty-five years, until they moved all the cooking to one big kitchen across the city.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get through the learning part at your age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: With my phone, honestly. I take a photo of the drawing, ask the AI app to explain it like I'm new, and it tells me what a joist hanger is or why the gap matters. I use it every day, on the bus, at lunch, at night to study for my carpentry certificate. My husband Marco drives a taxi and his money's dropped, and we helped our daughter with a rent deposit, so we've got barely three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, it's just a clever helper, and I'd keep showing the young ones how I use it to read drawings. Online I'd say that's fine, let's spend the money on warm homes instead of chasing robots. At work I'd laugh with Ollie that I'm still more tech than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep doing what I'm doing and my phone keeps being my teacher. That suits me. The hard part of my life is money and my knees, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the app every day and try to pass my certificate by next summer. I'd ask Greenfold if I can help train the other older starters on using these tools, maybe for a bit extra an hour. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bit disappointed, if I'm honest. I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because for me AI has been the best thing in years. It explained things I was too embarrassed to ask Ollie twice. If it stops there, fine, but I was hoping for a bit more, like help with my eyes reading tiny tape measure marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask to train other older starters. Do you think Greenfold would pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, they're not rich. But they lose good people in the first month because the drawings scare them, so a little extra an hour for me is cheaper than losing a starter. I'd make that case to the manager with numbers, and I'd get the app to help me write it.

S0.say: I'd say it's just a clever helper and keep showing the young ones how I use it to read drawings. The money should go on warm homes instead of chasing robots.
S0.think: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, with my phone as my teacher, and that suits me. The hard part of my life is money and my knees, not AI.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI app every day and aims to pass her carpentry certificate by next summer. Asks Greenfold to let her train older starters on these tools for a little extra pay.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little disappointed because she likes new things.
S0.quote: It explained things I was too embarrassed to ask Ollie twice.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is a rare late starter who sees AI as a personal tutor and would miss its growth. Her money is thin but her outlook here is relaxed. She already imagines turning her AI habit into a small paid role teaching others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for public money to help people retrain, and I'd say it loudly. Greenfold is a not-for-profit, so I'd push for them to bring the workers into the decisions about which tools to use. Online I'd share stories of people like me who learned late and made it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do all right, because retrofit work is only growing and AI helps me learn faster. It's Marco I worry about. Taxis are exactly the kind of job that shrinks in a picture like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for anything Greenfold offers on new tools, laser measuring, the planning apps, whatever comes. I'd sit with Marco and use the AI to look at what else he could do with a driving licence, maybe delivery vans for the council or driving a minibus for the care home. And I'd join the union branch that's starting at Greenfold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, excited. For us as a couple, a bit uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't wait until the fares are gone, look now. He's proud, and he thinks phones are for kids, so I'd have to sit next to him at the kitchen table and do it together. He'd grumble, then he'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the new tools worry you for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones that watch you. If the planning app starts timing how long I take to lay a board, I'll look bad, because I'm slow and I check twice. I want tools that teach me, not tools that report me.

S1.say: I'd say this is the time for public money to help people retrain. Greenfold, as a not-for-profit, should bring workers into decisions about new tools.
S1.think: I'd do all right, because retrofit work is only growing and AI helps me learn faster. It's Marco I worry about, because taxis are exactly the kind of job that shrinks.
S1.do: Signs up for every Greenfold course on new tools such as laser measuring and planning apps. Uses AI with her husband to look for driving jobs like council vans or a care home minibus, and joins the new union branch.
S1.feel: Excited for herself, uneasy for her and Marco as a couple.
S1.quote: He's proud, and he thinks phones are for kids, so I'd have to sit next to him at the kitchen table and do it together.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha's own outlook is bright here; the unease comes from her husband's exposed job. She'd use the same tools that helped her to help him. Her progressive views show in wanting workers to choose the tools, not just receive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a public plan right now, a basic income and free housing help, because nobody can prepare in two years. I'd say the robots should belong partly to the public if they're doing everyone's work. I'd be at the meetings, for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me, even me. I'd be sixty in 2028, still learning, and a robot that can fit floorboards won't need a trainee who checks the drawing on her phone. And Marco's taxi would be the first thing gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Greenfold and ask to be the person who works with the robots, setting them up, checking their work, talking to the families in the houses. Families still want a person in their home, I believe that. I'd also go to the council about help with rent, and I'd ask my son Teo, who's a nurse, if we could lean on him for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd want to be moving, not sitting. Sitting would be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think families would still want a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last week on Brook Street an old man, Mr Okafor, cried when we lifted his floor, because his wife had picked that carpet. I made him tea and listened for twenty minutes. No robot is doing that part, or if it is, I don't want to live in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With just two years, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever the robot makers put out, the instructions, the videos, before the robots even get to Brook Street. I'd stop eating out completely and sell the second phone Marco never uses. And I'd tell Teo honestly, we might need you, so it's not a surprise.

S2.say: I'd say we need a public plan now, a basic income and housing help, since nobody can prepare in two years. Robots doing everyone's work should partly belong to the public.
S2.think: It frightens me, even me. At sixty and still a trainee, a robot that can fit floorboards won't need me, and Marco's taxi would be the first thing gone.
S2.do: Asks Greenfold to make her the person who sets up and checks the robots and talks to the families. Goes to the council for rent help and asks her son Teo for support for a few months.
S2.feel: Scared, but wanting to be moving rather than sitting still.
S2.quote: No robot is doing that part, or if it is, I don't want to live in that world.
S2.fieldNote: Even adaptive Aisha is frightened by the two-year picture because she has no money and is still a trainee. Her bet is on the human side of home repair: being the person in the house. She mixes self-help with a clear call for public support and shared ownership of robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train everyone who wants it, so let's start now, with real money. I'd say Greenfold and builders like them should get funding to train older workers on the machines. I'd post that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better for me than people would guess. I'd be sixty-three, I'd have my certificate, and I'd have years of using AI tools behind me. I could be the one in the crew who knows both the old houses and the new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the AI to help me plan a course in home energy surveys, which you can do with a tablet and a thermal camera, and do it in the evenings within a year. I'd start doing small surveys for neighbours at weekends for a bit of money, twenty or thirty a time. And I'd put that money away, every bit of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more hopeful than scared. Five years is time to turn around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why energy surveys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because before you send any robot into a hundred-year-old house, someone has to walk round it, find the damp, find where the heat leaks. I already do half of that on Brook Street without the title. It's my eyes and my mouth, not my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years change for Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With five years he can do a course for driving a minibus or an ambulance, while there's still work like that. With two, he'd just sit in the taxi rank waiting for fares that don't come.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to train everyone who wants it, with real money. Builders like Greenfold should get funding to train older workers on the machines.
S3.think: Five years is better for me than people would guess. At sixty-three, with my certificate and years of using AI, I could be the one who knows both the old houses and the new machines.
S3.do: Uses AI to plan an evening course in home energy surveys within a year. Does small weekend surveys for neighbours at twenty or thirty each and saves every bit of it.
S3.feel: Nervous, but more hopeful than scared.
S3.quote: It's my eyes and my mouth, not my knees.
S3.fieldNote: Five years transforms Aisha's view: she sees time to move from her weak knees to her strengths in observation and talking to people. The side income is small but she'd bank it all. She stays anxious because the money is thin, but she sounds in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make this fair, so let's give every worker a training budget and a say. I'd say builders should share the savings from robots with the people they replace. I'd be the annoying one at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm sixty-eight, at pension age, and by then I could have five or six good years as a surveyor. I think I'd be fine. It's my kids and the young trainees who'd have the harder road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my certificate, then do the energy survey course, and ask Greenfold to make me a surveyor within three years. I'd help set up a training scheme for older starters, using the AI tools I already know. And I'd keep pushing the union for a share of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people waste them. With ten years everyone thinks there's no hurry, like Marco with his taxi, and then it's year nine. I'd tell anyone who'd listen: the time is a gift only if you open it early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be at pension age. Would you stop then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if my body lets me carry on. I'd do surveys part-time, three days a week maybe, because the pension on its own won't be much after the jobs I've had. And I like being useful, I always have.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make this fair, with a training budget and a say for every worker. Builders should share robot savings with the people they replace.
S4.think: I'd reach pension age with a few good years as a surveyor behind me, so I think I'd be fine. My kids and the young trainees would have the harder road.
S4.do: Finishes her certificate, takes the energy survey course and asks Greenfold to make her a surveyor within three years. Helps set up a training scheme for older starters and pushes the union for a share of the savings.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, even a little excited.
S4.quote: I'd tell anyone who'd listen: the time is a gift only if you open it early.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Aisha reach pension age with a planned move into surveying, so she's calm. Her one worry is people wasting the time, and she names her husband as an example. She keeps pairing her own adaptability with a demand that the gains be shared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to turn the boat round, and we've got no money in the boat. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, and free courses that let older people use what they're good at, like talking to families, instead of pretending we'll become engineers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what AI already did for them, not just what it might take. For me it was like having a patient teacher in my pocket when I started at fifty-five. Nobody else had that patience with me.

headlineQuote: For me it was like having a patient teacher in my pocket when I started at fifty-five.
portrait: Aisha Santos is a 58-year-old trainee carpenter at a not-for-profit builder that warms up old terraced houses, who came into building after twenty-five years as a school cook. She uses AI every day as her tutor and is the most upbeat person on her crew about new tools. Her calm turns to fear in the two-year AGI picture, where she has no savings and her husband's taxi work disappears too. With five or ten years she plans a move into energy surveying, using her eyes and her way with families rather than her knees, while pushing for gains to be shared.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there's no time to change course and no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income while people retrain, and free courses that build on what older workers are good at, like talking to families.
